A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Mixture-of-Memories work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: V1 reports original MoM experiments on recall, commonsense reasoning, LongBench, efficiency, and memory ablations, including detailed appendix results.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental results and adds hybrid-model, length-extrapolation, routing-analysis, and parameter-matched results.

M1.justification: V2 introduces a hybrid architecture with one Transformer layer after every seven MoM layers, totaling three Transformer layers within 24 layers (Section 4.2.4). This is a limited architectural extension; the original router, recurrent memory updates, memory mixing, and shared-memory mechanism remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 adds FineWeb evaluation and an explicit scenario testing generalization from 2K training contexts to lengths up to 32K (Section 4.2.7). SlimPajama training, the six recall tasks, commonsense benchmarks, and bilingual LongBench coverage are retained.

E2.justification: Corresponding main comparisons retain the same baseline memberships, including Transformer++, RetNet, HGRN2, GLA, GSA, and Gated DeltaNet. The expanded-memory comparison retains its GLA and Gated DeltaNet controls. New experiments reuse existing comparators; RWKV6 and RWKV7 appear only in the descriptive update-rule table.

E3.justification: V2 adds a control matching 400M activated parameters by reducing MoM's MLP hidden ratio to 2, length-extrapolation testing, and routing measurements on approximately 300K ARC-Easy tokens with and without auxiliary loss. Table 2 adds an average excluding FDA. The stated single-memory expansion changes from increasing both k and v dimensions to increasing v alone; this reporting revision does not establish that the earlier comparison was rerun.

E4.justification: V2 substantially expands analysis with length extrapolation, auxiliary-loss routing balance, token-specialization analysis, and an equal-activated-parameter control. These investigate generalization, memory utilization, and parameter-count confounding. The original memory-number/shared-memory ablations and training-loss analysis are retained, with the latter moved to Appendix E.

E5.justification: V1 Appendix C and v2 Appendix D both explicitly report a fixed seed of 42 and single-run results without aggregation across seeds. Neither version adds confidence intervals, significance tests, or other uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: V2 replaces the main 340M MoM results: recall average changes from 27.59 to 28.16, including FDA from 30.79 to 22.98, while commonsense average changes from 42.11 to 41.97 (Tables 2–3). The reason for these revisions is not explained. Substantial new results cover the hybrid model, parameter-matched control, expanded-memory commonsense comparison, extrapolation, and routing. The 1.3B, LongBench, and original ablation results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The core MoM equations and algebraic memory/query equivalence are retained. Removing the standard softmax-attention primer and adding RWKV examples to Table 1 changes mathematical exposition, without introducing new theoretical assumptions, derivations, proofs, or formal properties.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same claims: multiple memories increase capacity and reduce or eliminate interference, preserve linear-model efficiency, and improve recall performance toward Transformer levels. The added experiments do not redefine these central claims.

C2.justification: V2 interprets memory routing as specialization into different semantic roles and attributes improved routing balance to auxiliary loss (Section 4.2.8 and Table 7). Appendix F newly acknowledges the difficulty of simultaneously matching parameters and memory capacity, and the possible commonsense cost of reducing MLP width. The original interference explanation remains intact.

D1.justification: V2 clarifies nominal model-size labels and activated-parameter accounting, supplies parameter counts for expanded-memory comparisons, and documents the hybrid layer arrangement and reduced MLP ratio for the 400M control. Auxiliary loss is newly mentioned without its formula or coefficient. Code-access information, hardware, training times, and the existing optimizer and training-budget details are retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds the FineWeb citation to Penedo et al. (2024), includes RWKV6/7 in Table 1, and introduces a contrast between MoM memory specialization and conventional FFN-based MoE specialization. The existing related-work discussion and MoM–MoE distinction are retained in Appendices A and B.

P1.justification: V2 removes the softmax-attention primer, relocates Related Work and Training Loss Comparison to appendices, and adds parameter explanations and acknowledgments. Some headings and wording are refined. Most existing prose, including the abstract, introduction, core method, and conclusion, remains unchanged.

P2.justification: V2 adds the extrapolation plot, paired routing heatmaps, and hybrid, memory-function, and parameter-matched tables. The expanded-memory table gains parameter counts and a commonsense panel, while Table 2 gains an FDA-excluding average column. The original training-loss plot is relocated from Figure 3 to Figure 5; the architecture and efficiency figures are essentially retained.

improvement.justification: V2 improves experimental credibility through explicit parameter accounting and the matched-400M control, partly addressing parameter-count confounding in v1. Table 9 supports a recall advantage of 26.51 versus 24.78, alongside only a 0.06-point commonsense gap. Extrapolation and routing analyses add useful validation. However, unexplained differences between revised main results and retained ablation rows, incomplete auxiliary-loss details, and unchanged single-run reporting limit the overall gain.
